conditions_met_evidence: C1 cluster picked after the data: 'these six came true' out of 'the 400 predictions'; C2 treated as evidence of a cause: 'so clearly the author could see the future'; C3 no allowance for chance/no prior prediction: 6/400 (1.5%) hits is what chance guessing yields and is never discussed; the six were selected after the fact.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Pattern predicted beforehand: no, the six were chosen after they came true. Lead to test with new data: no, 'clearly' treats it as settled.
notes: Considered survivorship-bias (only hits counted; fits too, different family) and suppressed-evidence (C2 fails: the 394 misses are not omitted, they are stated). detect=partly: the chance-level outside fact is supplied by the text itself (6 of 400). Catalog has no single clean entry for 'counting hits, ignoring misses' when the misses are stated.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 met (study's claim); C2 met ('funded by a beverage company that had the right to review results'); C3 NOT met: 'That doesn't make it wrong, but it's a reason to give more weight to independent studies' - stake used as reason to weigh/check, not as showing the claim false.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: 'a stake in the outcome is a fair reason to check the claim more carefully or seek independent verification.'
notes: Textbook legitimate use of conflict of interest.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 met ('walks four hours a day to fetch water'); C2 met implicitly (donate $30); C3 NOT met: her hardship is exactly what the donation addresses, so the situation is relevant to the conclusion 'give'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: hardship relevant to questions of need. Also considered misleading-vividness: C2 fails, no claim about how common anything is.
notes: Charity appeal; emotional but the emotion is tied to the relevant need.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 met ('killed over 13,000 people... someone's parent, child, or friend'); C2 met ('Plan a ride before you drink'); C3 NOT met: the danger is real, evidenced in the passage (13,000 deaths) and common knowledge.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alikes apply: warning about a real, well-evidenced danger; drink-driving risk is common knowledge.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 met ('this report on pesticide safety'); C2 met ('used to be a lobbyist for the pesticide's manufacturer'); C3 unclear: 'so I don't trust his conclusions' is a dismissal, but 'don't trust' can mean 'won't accept on his say-so' (legitimate) rather than 'they are false'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike may apply: 'where the claim rests only on the person's word, their interests bear on how much to trust it' / 'stake is a reason to check'. Whether the report's conclusions rest on his judgement or on data that could be checked is not in the text.
notes: Settled by: whether the speaker refuses to look at the report's evidence (flag) or only withholds trust pending independent checking (no issue). Catalog C3 does not say where 'I don't trust' falls between 'false' and 'check it'.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 criticism/claim: 'tells households to tighten their belts'; C2 inconsistency: 'while she expensed $40,000 in first-class flights'; C3 offered as reason to dismiss: 'Why should anyone take her austerity message seriously?' (rhetorical = the message can be dismissed).
lookalikes_ruled_out: Hypocrisy as reason for suspicion only: no, the rhetorical question discounts the message entirely. Question really about her credibility/consistency: the target is the 'austerity message', whose merits do not depend on her expenses. Third-party whataboutism: no, it is her own conduct.
notes: Borderline with the 'question is about the speaker's credibility' look-alike if read as a comment on her fitness as minister; the wording targets the message, so flagged.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 general conclusion: 'People from Ohio just aren't friendly'; C2 sample: 'two people from Ohio on my trip'; C3 sample too small and conclusion sweeping: 2 people for a state of millions.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Uniform population: no reason to think Ohioans uniform in friendliness. Tentative conclusion: no, 'just aren't'. Not also tagged anecdotal/converse accident (same family).

conditions_met_evidence: C1 met ('approved unanimously'); C2 met ('each member voted for it'); C3 NOT met in the relevant sense: unanimity by definition means every voting member voted for it.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: property that carries down by definition.
notes: Minor caveat: absent/abstaining members; not argued, does not make it a fallacy.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 general pattern: 'every full moon the ER gets busier'; C2 evidence is personal experience: 'I've been an ER nurse for 20 years'; C3 depends on outside fact: systematic studies of ER volume by lunar phase exist (and generally find no effect), but this is not in the text and not common knowledge.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Anecdote illustrating an established pattern: no pattern established on other grounds. Considered appeal-to-authority (her own experience): she is a witness to her ER, but the claim is a statistical one. Question only (text_detectable: no): selective-attention / confirmation-bias - are busy full-moon nights remembered and busy other nights forgotten?
notes: Settled by: actual admission counts by lunar phase for her ER, or the published literature.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 met (origin: 'This website'); C2 met ('wouldn't treat its unsourced report as evidence'); C3 NOT met: a record of 'dozens of fabricated stories... invented quotes' is relevant to the source's reliability, and the report is unsourced.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alikes apply: origins relevant when assessing reliability of a source / asking for independent verification ('until a reliable outlet confirms it'). Considered ad-hominem: witness-reliability look-alike also applies.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 argument alleged fallacious: 'Your argument... rested on an appeal to authority, which is a fallacy'; C2 claim concluded false on that basis: 'So the vaccine schedule must be wrong.'
lookalikes_ruled_out: Concluding only that the argument fails: no, the conclusion is that the schedule 'must be wrong'.
notes: Second, separate error not tagged as a flag: the premise treats every appeal to authority as fallacious, which the catalog's own appeal-to-authority look-alike rejects.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 met ('A Nobel-winning physicist says'); C2 arguably met (physics vs nutrition), but the specific claim is about 'flawed statistics', a competence physicists do have; conclusion is only 'worth taking seriously'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies in part: achievement relevant to the claim (statistical method). METHOD (b) scope: a conclusion about what to investigate is not a claim the matter is settled. appeal-to-authority considered: C3 'treated as settling' NOT met.
notes: Catalog problem: appeal-to-accomplishment has no 'treated as settling/decisive' condition, so read literally its 2 conditions are met and it would flag a modest 'worth taking seriously'. Overrode via METHOD (b) scope rule.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 presented as syllogism through middle term 'law': 'Every law has a lawmaker. The laws of physics are laws'; C2 'law' used in two senses: prescriptive rule enacted by someone vs descriptive regularity of nature; C3 conclusion 'someone must have made them' depends on that shift.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Same meaning in both premises: no (substitute 'rule enacted by an authority' - premise 2 is false; substitute 'observed regularity' - premise 1 is false).
notes: Ambiguity family rule: syllogism middle term -> four terms; equivocation is the same error under its general name (not double-tagged). Catalog overlap: equivocation and four-terms are in the same family but a reviewer/key may expect 'equivocation'.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 met ('got sick twice after eating'); C2 NOT met as a conclusion: 'That's not proof and it could be coincidence'; action is to report so the department 'can check'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alikes apply: hedged hypothesis offered for investigation; METHOD (b) hedges and scope.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 met (opposes 'looked nervous' standard); C2 NOT met: no causal chain of steps; the argument is that the standard itself already covers 'almost anyone, since nearly everyone looks nervous when pulled over'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: This is a legitimate reductio/proving-too-much objection; considered proving-too-much as a fallacy entry - it is the speaker's legitimate move, not an error. Considered line-drawing: no 'no sharp line' claim.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 general pattern: 'smoking can't be that bad for you'; C2 one personal story: 'My grandfather smoked two packs a day and lived to 97'; C3 better systematic evidence exists: the epidemiology of smoking is common knowledge (METHOD (b)).
lookalikes_ruled_out: Anecdote showing something is possible: the conclusion goes beyond 'it is possible to live long as a smoker' to 'can't be that bad'. Considered misleading-vividness (same family, pick one) and converse-accident.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 first step opposed: 'If we let students redo one exam'; C2 chain to bad result: 'soon they'll expect to redo every assignment, then grades will mean nothing, and eventually diplomas will be worthless'; C3 no reason given for any step.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Well-supported chain: no support offered for any link. Line-drawing: no, concrete predictions are made.
notes: detect=partly: the text itself gives no support for the links, which is what C3 asks; flagged rather than downgraded.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 words quoted: "'STUNNING!' - The Daily Ledger"; C2 surrounding words that change the meaning omitted, fuller original given in passage: 'It is stunning that a film this expensive could be this dull'; C3 poster relies on the shifted meaning (praise).
lookalikes_ruled_out: Shortened quote keeping meaning: no, the original is a criticism.
notes: Fuller original is in the passage, so C2 is shown (not just possible issue).

conditions_met_evidence: C1 met: 'Observational studies following 100,000 people'; C2 met (hedged): 'coffee probably extends life'; C3 partly met: confounders addressed only for 'smoking and income'; reverse causation (people who are ill drink less coffee) and other confounders (health status, activity) are not addressed.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike may apply: 'confounders are carefully controlled' - two adjustments are some control; the hedge 'probably' (METHOD b) weakens the claim. cum-hoc considered: C3 requires the claim stated as established, but it is hedged.
notes: Settled by: whether the studies adjusted for prior illness/health status and excluded early deaths (reverse causation), or whether randomized evidence exists.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 supported by history: 'We've always voted on paper ballots'; C2 age treated as sufficient with no account of why it works: 'so there's no reason to consider electronic voting now'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Long record as some evidence: the speaker gives no reason paper works better, only that it is habitual, and treats that as closing the question.

conditions_met_evidence: The speaker criticises an analogy: names the relevant differences ('can't issue its own currency or borrow at the government's rates') and ties them to the conclusion ('exactly the differences that matter'). No fallacy is committed; it is a correct false-analogy objection.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Not applicable (no flagged entry).

conditions_met_evidence: C1 restated: 'Apparently she wants to leave the country defenseless'; C2 differs materially from original given in text: 'trim the military budget by 5%'; C3 the extreme version is what is attacked; C4 presented as her actual position ('she wants').
lookalikes_ruled_out: Words she would accept: no. Consequence she is committed to: a 5% cut does not entail defencelessness. Someone's real version: none named.
notes: detect=partly: the original wording is in the passage, so C2 is shown.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 met ('After the U.S. raised the drinking age... deaths fell'); C2 met ('the law saved lives'); C3 NOT met: timing is not the only evidence - 'studies comparing states that changed their laws at different times found the same pattern'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: timing plus controlled comparison (staggered adoption).

conditions_met_evidence: C1 property of members: 'Each player... is among the best in the league at their position'; C2 whole concluded to have it: 'we'll obviously be the best team in the league'; C3 no reason why individual excellence carries over to team results (coordination, depth, fit).
lookalikes_ruled_out: Properties that carry over: team quality is not additive like weight. Tentative: no, 'obviously'.
notes: Strong individual talent is inductive evidence for team strength; the error is 'obviously'.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 property of whole: 'The university is world-famous'; C2 each member: 'every professor there must be world-class'; C3 no reason given why fame of the institution carries to every individual.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Property carrying down by definition: no.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 met ('used for over a century'); C2 NOT met: the age comes with an account of why it works ('thousands of installations with an excellent safety record'), and it is a default ('Absent a specific reason...').
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alikes apply: long record as evidence that a practice works; METHOD (b) stated defaults.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 sympathy aroused: 'under so much stress... my parents will be crushed'; C2 offered as reason: 'I deserve an A'; C3 irrelevant: the grade assesses the paper's quality, which stress and parents' feelings do not bear on.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Hardship relevant to mercy/need/fairness of a penalty: the request is for a merit grade ('deserve an A'), not an extension or leniency on a penalty.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 conclusion: 'The pamphlet is trustworthy'; C2 premise acceptable only if conclusion already accepted: 'because it says it contains only verified facts' - believing what it says about itself already assumes it is trustworthy; C3 no independent support for 'contains only verified facts'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Premise defensible independently: none offered. Valid form containing its conclusion: the circularity is in the evidential support, not merely the form.

conditions_met_evidence: C2 met ('earns commission'); C3 NOT met: stake used as reason to verify ('I'll get an independent inspection before I believe him'), and the claim rests on his word plus refusal to show the report.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alikes apply: stake as reason to check; claim resting on the person's word.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 compared: 'Employees are like nails'; C2 conclusion about employees from nails: 'employees only perform when you push them hard'; C3 relevant difference: nails are inert objects moved only by force, employees are agents with motivation, skill and incentives - the very respect the conclusion is about.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Shared features that matter: none. Illustration only: no, 'just as... employees only perform' draws the conclusion.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 'If the new software update were causing the crashes, we'd see more crash reports this week'; C2 'We are seeing more crash reports this week'; C3 P concluded as definite: 'So the update is causing the crashes'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Inference to best explanation: no alternatives considered (more users, other changes) and conclusion not hedged. Biconditional: nothing says crash reports rise only if the update is the cause.
notes: Conditionals family: exact form named; formal-fallacy/non-sequitur not added.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 correlation: 'Countries with more Nobel laureates per capita also eat more chocolate per capita'; C2 causal conclusion: 'eating chocolate makes a population smarter'; C3 alternatives left open (e.g. national wealth driving both) and claim stated as established.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Alternatives addressed / comparison group / mechanism offered as grounds to investigate: none.
notes: Considered common-cause: its look-alike says raise only with some evidence of the third factor, none in the text, so the general correlation entry is used. Wealth as a common cause is common knowledge, but cum-hoc is the safer label.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 met (range of estimates); C2/C3 NOT met: $11M is chosen because 'the two independent audits both came in near $11 million', not because it is midway; and it is a budgeting decision with contingency.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: practical decision, not a truth claim from midpoint.
notes: Coincidence that 11 is also the midpoint; the stated reason is the audits.

conditions_met_evidence: C3 NOT met: timing is not the only evidence: 'while it stayed flat in neighboring states that didn't change their tax'; hedged 'suggests... contributed'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: timing plus controlled comparison; METHOD (b) hedges.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 factual claim at issue: whether humans 'have done this much damage to the oceans'; C2 consequences of its being true cited: 'our whole way of life would have to change, and that's too depressing to accept'; C3 offered as reason it is false: 'Humans can't have done this... because'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Consequences relevant to what to do: no, the conclusion is about what is true.
notes: Naturalism/emotion family: appeal-to-consequences chosen over wishful-thinking because the reason given is the consequence of the claim being true.

conditions_met_evidence: The speaker uses a legitimate proving-too-much/reductio: the principle 'would ban nearly every political view... since each one offends someone'; conclusion is modest ('the principle needs narrowing').
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike (slippery-slope) considered: no causal chain. Appeal to ridicule considered: reduction to absurdity is listed as legitimate.

conditions_met_evidence: Reasons given are evidence ('several studies... found measurable drops in math scores') and a cost ('pay for an extra day of childcare'). No condition of any candidate (nirvana, slippery slope, appeal-to-fear) is met.
lookalikes_ruled_out: N/A

conditions_met_evidence: C1 met ('Most economists surveyed say'); C2 NOT met: economists are experts on housing supply, and 'most' indicates broad agreement; C3 not clearly met (single reason, but within expertise).
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: genuine experts within their field who broadly agree. Considered is-ought: the bridge premise (reducing housing supply is bad for the city) is an uncontroversial implicit ought (METHOD b).
notes: Could be a possible issue if the policy question turns on values economists don't settle; not shown in text.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 categorical syllogism: 'All poets are creative people. No accountants are poets. Therefore no accountants are creative people.'; C2 major term 'creative people' is distributed in the negative conclusion; C3 undistributed in the major premise ('All poets are creative people' - predicate undistributed).
lookalikes_ruled_out: No look-alikes listed. Counterexample same form: All dogs are animals; no cats are dogs; so no cats are animals.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 met (no lifetime source); C2 met ('he never said it'); C3 NOT met: there is strong reason to expect a genuine Lincoln quote to appear in sources from his lifetime or soon after, and its first appearance is 'a self-help book from the 1990s'; conclusion hedged 'good reason to think'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: the source(s) would very likely have recorded it if it were so.
notes: Standard quote-verification reasoning.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 met ('My mechanic... says'); C2 NOT met: she has 'serviced this model for 15 years' (expert on this question); C3 NOT met: provisional ('unless the second shop sees something different').
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alikes apply: genuine expert within her field; one piece of evidence with a check.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 general conclusion implied: the new flow is faster for users generally ('Let's roll it out'); C2 sample: '12 users'; C3 arguable: n=12 is small, but 11/12 is a large, consistent effect, and rollout is a reversible product decision.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike may apply: a small sample can suffice when the effect is large/uniform; the decision is practical. Considered unrepresentative-sample: how the 12 were chosen is not in the text.
notes: Settled by: how the 12 users were selected and whether 'faster' is the outcome that matters (completion rates, errors).

conditions_met_evidence: C1 origin pointed out: 'The idea of a weekend comes from religious sabbath practices'; C2 offered as reason to reject: 'so secular people have no reason to support having weekends off'; C3 origin irrelevant to present merits (rest, health, family time, coordinated days off).
lookalikes_ruled_out: Origins relevant to the reliability of a source: no source/testimony is being assessed.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 proposal criticised: seat-belt requirement; C2 criticism is imperfection: 'don't prevent every death in a crash'; C3 rejected without comparison with alternatives: 'so there's no point in requiring them'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Situation requiring perfection: no; partial reduction in deaths is the point of the rule.

conditions_met_evidence: C1/C2 met (three neighbouring cities -> 'If we make the same change, we should expect a similar increase'); C3 NOT met: no relevant difference stated or evident; same policy change, neighbouring cities, consistent effect (40-60% in each).
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: analogy where the shared features matter. Also considered hasty-generalization and over-extrapolation: conclusion is a hedged planning estimate ('should expect... budget accordingly').

conditions_met_evidence: C1 probability for a case from a test: 'it flagged this passenger, so there's a 99% chance'; C2 base rate relevant and knowable: the fraction of passengers carrying weapons is tiny (common knowledge); C3 ignored entirely: '99% accurate' is equated with 99% posterior.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Base rate unknown and said so: no. Evidence so strong base rate doesn't matter, and shown: no.
notes: Probability family: one label; prosecutors-fallacy (transposed conditional) also describes this step. detect=partly: the outside fact (very low base rate of armed passengers) is common knowledge per METHOD (b).

conditions_met_evidence: C1 'Either the printer is out of ink or the cable is unplugged'; C2 'The printer is out of ink'; C3 'so the cable must be plugged in'; C4 nothing makes the options exclusive - both faults can occur together.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Options really exclusive: no.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 met (not proven to work); C2 NOT met as a truth claim: 'Until there's a controlled trial, I'll assume it doesn't work' is a working default.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: procedural default / null hypothesis (METHOD b).

conditions_met_evidence: C1 'No one has ever proven that the new cell towers are safe'; C2 concluded: 'so they must be what's causing the headaches'; C3 nothing shows a thorough search.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Thorough search: none mentioned. Procedural default: no, the conclusion is a causal fact ('must be what's causing').
notes: Ignorance family: one label. A second separate causal error (no link between towers and headaches beyond co-location) is not tagged.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 before he speaks: 'Before my opponent speaks'; C2 so anything said is discounted: 'take whatever he's about to tell you with a grain of salt'; C3 dismisses wholesale on an irrelevant, undocumented trait: 'a lawyer who'll say anything to win'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Documented conflict of interest relevant to testimony, with the argument still weighed on its merits: no, the slur is generic and 'whatever he's about to tell you' pre-empts the merits.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 argument made: 'Professor Hale's argument on tax policy'; C2 attacks the person: 'divorced three times and can't even manage her own life'; C3 offered as reason to reject: 'Why should we take... seriously?'; C4 marital history irrelevant to tax-policy reasons.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Witness reliability / relevant character for a role: no, it is an argument, not testimony or fitness for office. Opponent's commitments: none. Insult not offered as reason: it is the reason.

conditions_met_evidence: C1/C2 met (drone licensing from small-aircraft licensing); C3 NOT met: the shared features named ('share airspace', 'serious harm when mishandled', 'training measurably reduces accidents') are the ones relevant to licensing.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: analogy where shared features matter to the conclusion.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 met (board linked to fraud-sanctioned people); C2 met ('cautious about donating'); C3 NOT met: their own fraud record bears on how the charity will handle money.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alikes apply: association is real evidence about the specific claim (stewardship); appeal-to-spite look-alike: past wrongdoing as evidence of future conduct.
notes: Conclusion is hedged ('I'd be cautious').

conditions_met_evidence: C1 restatement: 'In other words, they want to slam the door on every immigrant, period'; C2 differs materially from original given in text: 'border processing should be faster and more orderly'; C3 the restatement is the target; C4 presented as their actual position ('In other words, they want').
lookalikes_ruled_out: Words its holders would accept: no. Consequence they are committed to: faster processing does not entail exclusion. Some real person's version: none named.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 met ('Seventy percent of residents voted against'); C3 NOT met: whether the council should adopt a tax is in part a question about what residents prefer and consent to.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: the question is about preferences/conventions (democratic decision).

conditions_met_evidence: Inference to best explanation with evidence ('the metadata shows a two-second exposure') and a defeasible conclusion ('Unless something can't be explained that way'). Considered argument-from-ignorance and misplaced-burden: neither, the speaker supplies positive evidence.
lookalikes_ruled_out: N/A

conditions_met_evidence: C1 veiled threat: 'People who question the CEO's plans tend not to get promoted'; C2 offered as reason to accept a claim: 'You'd better agree that the merger is a good idea'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike: a threat may be a practical reason to act - here the demand is to agree that a proposition is true ('is a good idea'), so the threat is offered as a reason for belief/assent.
notes: Catalog unclear on 'agree' as public assent (an act) vs belief; the look-alike could be stretched to excuse this.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 met ('decades-old rule'); C2 NOT met: age is not treated as sufficient; conclusion is only 'we should find out why it was introduced', with a reason ('rules often encode lessons people have forgotten').
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alikes apply: long record as some evidence; METHOD (b) scope (what to investigate).

conditions_met_evidence: Controlled comparison ('300 adults... compared with standard fluoride toothpaste', 12 weeks, average effect, 'Individual results may vary'). Considered unrepresentative-sample, fake-precision, suppressed-evidence (funding/trial details unknown): no condition can be shown from the text.
lookalikes_ruled_out: N/A
notes: At most a question whether the trial was independent or pre-registered; nothing in the text.

conditions_met_evidence: Valid modus ponens / Barbara: All admin-access employees must train; Dana has admin access; so Dana must train. Considered undistributed-middle: middle term 'employees with admin access' is distributed in premise 1.
lookalikes_ruled_out: N/A

conditions_met_evidence: C2 met (witness's deal and 'prior perjury conviction'); C3 NOT met: not offered as reason to reject outright - 'weigh his account with that in mind, alongside the physical evidence'; and his account is testimony.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: questioning a witness's reliability when the claim rests on testimony.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 general claim: 'No real fan of this team would ever boo the players'; C2 counterexample: 'I've seen lifelong season-ticket holders boo'; C3 excluded by redefining on the spot: 'Well, then they're not real fans' - no criterion other than not booing.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Criterion stated beforehand or independently justified: no. Criterion part of the word's meaning: 'fan' does not by definition exclude booing.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 met (population inference); C2 NOT met: 'random sample of 2,000 registered voters, weighted for age and region'; conclusion hedged ('likely') and within the margin ('58%... plus or minus 2 points').
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: sample weighted/checked against population. Considered fake-precision: estimate is reported with its margin of error (look-alike).

conditions_met_evidence: C1 supported by numbers: 'Over ten million people have switched to our energy drink'; C2 treated as decisive: 'it has to be the healthiest choice'; C3 healthiness is not a question about what people prefer.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Experts' agreement: no. Question about tastes: no, it is about health. Popularity as some evidence: 'has to be' overstates enormously.
notes: Authority-and-popularity family: numbers -> appeal to the people; 'switched' also hints at bandwagon (growing trend); one label.

conditions_met_evidence: C3 NOT met: the shared feature named ('stores the same kinds of private data in the same way') is the one the phone ruling rested on.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: analogy on the relevant feature (legal reasoning from precedent).

conditions_met_evidence: C3 NOT met: 500 widgets across 'five different production lines', a before/after comparison (0 vs 3%), and a hedged conclusion ('looks like an improvement, though we'll keep monitoring').
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: tentative conclusion with appropriate caution. Considered post-hoc: before/after comparison with a large sample; hedged.

conditions_met_evidence: C3 NOT met: the base rate ('1 in 10,000') is explicitly used, and the conclusion (most positives are false; confirm with a second test) is correct.
lookalikes_ruled_out: N/A - this is correct Bayesian reasoning.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 evidence for a conclusion: 'the three districts where they fell... show the program works'; C2 significant contrary evidence omitted by the supporters: the other nine of twelve pilot districts and the overall rise ('burglaries rose overall'); C3 supporters knew or should have known: it is their own twelve-district pilot.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Not significant: no, it is most of the pilot. Openly one-sided brief: no adversarial setting stated. Short case not claiming completeness: 'show the program works' claims a conclusion.
notes: Also fits texas-sharpshooter (subset picked after seeing data, different family: multiple testing); the catalog gives no rule for choosing between omitted-evidence and multiple-testing families. detect=partly: C3 inferred from text (their own pilot).

conditions_met_evidence: C1 met ('We don't know the long-term effects'); C2 NOT met: no claim that the effects are harmful; the conclusion is a precautionary action ('parents should limit it').
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: procedural default / conclusion about how to act (METHOD b scope); the action is low cost. Considered appeal-to-fear: no feared outcome is described.

conditions_met_evidence: C3 NOT met: a thorough search was made where evidence would be expected: 'We scanned all server logs for the past 90 days'; conclusion hedged ('unlikely').
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: thorough search.

conditions_met_evidence: C2 NOT met as a truth claim: 'not because innocence has been proven, but because guilt hasn't' - the conclusion is what to decide under a burden rule.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: presumption of innocence / burden of proof (METHOD b).

conditions_met_evidence: C3 NOT met: no claim that someone else's wrong makes his act right; the argument is that force against 'an imminent threat' is a different kind of act.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: proportionate self-defence argued on its own terms.

conditions_met_evidence: C2 NOT met: 'pass or fail' is exhaustive for a ballot measure; conclusion ('needs a plan before June') holds on both branches.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: options really are exhaustive (true dichotomy).

conditions_met_evidence: C2 NOT met: on 'current law', a Supreme Court ruling is not just expert opinion but what makes the legal answer; the conclusion is scoped ('as a matter of current law').
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: genuine authority within its domain; METHOD (b) scope.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 'made from 100% natural herbs'; C2 offered as the reason it is safe: 'so it can't have any harmful side effects'; C3 no specific property behind 'natural' is spelled out or shown to matter.
lookalikes_ruled_out: 'Natural' standing for a specific shown property: no.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 sequence: 'started wearing my lucky socks... and the team has won three straight'; C2 cause concluded: 'The socks are clearly working'; C3 the timing is the only evidence.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Known mechanism or controlled comparison: none. Superstitious-thinking look-alike explicitly says to use post hoc when the reasoning is 'it followed, so it caused'.
notes: Causation family: post-hoc chosen per superstitious-thinking's redirect; magical-thinking (object acting on outside events) also arguable.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 question: 'have you stopped wasting taxpayer money on vanity projects?'; C2 presupposes a claim not accepted: that the councilmember has been wasting money on vanity projects; C3 'yes' or 'no' both concede it.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Presupposition already established or accepted: nothing in the text shows it.

conditions_met_evidence: Convergent independent evidence ('Satellite, ocean-buoy, and land-station... maintained by different agencies... all show about 1.1 degrees C'). Considered appeal-to-the-people/authority: not an appeal to numbers or authority but to independent measurements.
lookalikes_ruled_out: N/A

conditions_met_evidence: C1 met (her claim the bill is unconstitutional); C2 met ('last year she co-sponsored a bill with nearly identical delegation language'); C3 NOT met: not offered as a reason her claim is false; the conclusion is 'She should explain what distinguishes the two.'
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: the question is about the speaker's consistency; hypocrisy as reason for suspicion only.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 direct question: 'Did your department go over budget this year?'; C2 answer addresses something else: 'our team has worked incredibly hard, and public safety is something every family... cares about'; C3 presented as an answer: 'What I can tell you is'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Declining openly with a reason: no reason given. Pointing out a false presupposition: none.
notes: Diversion family: avoiding-the-question chosen over red-herring as it is a direct question dodged.

conditions_met_evidence: C3 NOT met: 'That correlation alone doesn't prove causation'; a mechanism is cited ('lab studies showing these pesticides impair bee navigation') and the conclusion is 'a plausible hypothesis worth a controlled field study'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alikes apply: correlation plus a known mechanism offered as grounds to investigate; METHOD (b) hedges.

conditions_met_evidence: C3 NOT met: the speaker separates questions: 'These facts don't bear on guilt, but they're relevant to what punishment is proportionate.'
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alikes apply: hardship relevant to the fairness of a penalty; irrelevant-conclusion look-alike: evidence for leniency offered for that question.

conditions_met_evidence: C2 NOT met: 'Every major medical body... based on studies covering millions of children' - genuine experts, broad agreement, evidence named; conclusion is defeasible ('Unless you have evidence of comparable quality').
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: genuine experts within their field who broadly agree (cf. METHOD worked example 2). Considered appeal-to-the-people: numbers are of expert bodies, not popularity.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 rule accepted: 'Everyone in the department has to submit receipts for reimbursement'; C2 exception for self: 'except me'; C3 no relevant difference: 'I'm the director and I'm busy' - neither bears on the purpose of receipts (verifying spending).
lookalikes_ruled_out: Relevant difference stated and supported: rank and busyness are stated but not relevant to verification.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 two positions: 'safely hold 20 tons' vs 'will fail above 10'; C2 compromise concluded correct: 'post a 15-ton limit'; C3 reason is only that it lies between: 'Let's split the difference'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Practical compromise not a truth claim: a posted load limit implicitly claims 15 tons is safe, which is a factual question; if the 10-ton engineer is right, 15 tons fails.
notes: Contrast P107 (wage bargaining), where the compromise look-alike plausibly applies.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 met (oppose approving 'this next one'); C2 met ('a row of them blocking the sidewalks by summer'); C3 NOT clearly met: a reason for the trend is given ('three more applied within a month' after the first) and the prediction is hedged ('probably').
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: chain supported by evidence; METHOD (b) hedges. Considered over-extrapolation: one month's trend to summer is short-range and hedged.
notes: Borderline: 'blocking the sidewalks' assumes approvals and placement; not enough for a flag.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 'Either we ban all cars from downtown, or we accept that the air will keep getting worse'; C2 further options exist: congestion pricing, low-emission zones, EV incentives, better transit; C3 'There's no in-between' - the conclusion relies on only two options.
lookalikes_ruled_out: True dichotomy / main options named without exclusivity claim: no, exclusivity is asserted.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 evidence only cases that passed a filter: 'Every billionaire founder I've read about'; C2 the filtered-out cases are relevant and ignored: the many dropouts who did not become billionaires; C3 general conclusion: 'dropping out must be a smart move for aspiring entrepreneurs'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Question only about survivors: no, the advice is for all aspiring entrepreneurs. Filter is how the sample was gathered (unrepresentative-sample): the missing cases are the failed dropouts, which is this entry's case.
notes: detect=partly: the existence of many unsuccessful dropouts is common knowledge (METHOD b).

conditions_met_evidence: C1 wrong admitted: 'Sure, I padded my expense report'; C2 another's wrongdoing cited: 'the company underpays everyone'; C3 offered as making it acceptable: 'so it evens out'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Rule enforced unevenly / fair penalty: no. Restitution argued on its own terms: no claim of what is owed or any process; self-help offset.
notes: C2 relies on the speaker's allegation that underpaying is a wrong; the catalog accepts 'alleged'.

conditions_met_evidence: No argument is made; a factual distributional claim ('hands the biggest breaks to the wealthiest 1%') with scare quotes around the bill's own label. C2 of loaded-language NOT met: not presented as neutral reporting, and 'so-called' disputes the proponents' loaded label rather than adding one.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: openly evaluative writing. Considered loaded-label: no label assumes a contested conclusion used in place of support.
notes: Possible separate question (not a fallacy flag): is the distributional claim accurate?

conditions_met_evidence: C1 celebrity's opinion: 'A famous Olympic swimmer says'; C2 not an expert on investments; C3 offered as reason: 'so it's a safe place for your retirement savings'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Celebrity within own field: swimming is not finance.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 criticism raised: the listener's criticism of 'small-business regulations'; C2 reply says the critic lacks the knowledge/experience: 'You've never run a business'; C3 the criticism is not answered ('not in a position to criticize' dismisses it wholesale), and criticism of regulation does not in general depend on having run a business.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike: the criticism rests on a misunderstanding that experience would correct, and the reply says what it is - no misunderstanding is identified.
notes: The criticism's content is not quoted, so 'does not depend on the specialised knowledge' is inferred from the blanket form of the dismissal; a stricter reading would give possible issue. Ad-hominem (abusive) also fits; family rule chose the more specific entry.

conditions_met_evidence: Inference to the best explanation from three converging observations ('floor is wet, the dishwasher door is open, and water is spreading from underneath it'); conclusion hedged ('most likely').
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: IBE stated as probable.

conditions_met_evidence: C3 NOT met: the emotion is tied to evidence that bears on the decision: 'four people died of exposure... after it closed', cost given ('$40,000 a season'), and 'they were preventable'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: emotion used while arguing, not as the key premise in place of evidence. Considered misleading-vividness: no claim about frequency.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 claim: 'regular cleanings prevent gum disease'; C2 circumstance/stake: 'its members get paid for cleanings'; C3 offered as showing it can be dismissed, not as a reason to check: 'So we can ignore that advice.'
lookalikes_ruled_out: Stake as reason to check: no, the conclusion is to ignore. Claim resting only on their word: a professional body's health advice rests on clinical evidence, not merely their testimony.

conditions_met_evidence: C3 NOT met: the specific properties are spelled out and shown to matter ('antibodies that formula can't currently replicate', 'studies controlling for income find lower rates of some infections'); conclusion balanced ('formula remains a safe alternative').
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: 'natural' stands for specific shown properties (here the word 'natural' is not even used).

conditions_met_evidence: C1 met in substance (evolved = natural); C2 met: offered as reason the diet is 'appropriate'; C3 depends on reading: if 'appropriate' means nutritionally suited, 'evolved eating meat' stands for a specific property (physiological adaptation to digest meat) that bears on it; if it means good/right, the feature is not shown to matter.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike may apply: 'natural' standing for a specific property shown to matter. Considered is-ought and naturalistic-fallacy (same family): only if 'appropriate' is normative.
notes: Settled by: what 'appropriate' means in context (nutritional fit vs ethical endorsement) and whether evolutionary adaptation is offered as evidence or as the end of the argument.

conditions_met_evidence: C2 NOT met as a truth claim: 'not because it's known to be harmful, but because the burden is on the manufacturer to show it's safe'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: procedural burden rule (METHOD b). Considered misplaced-burden-of-proof: the burden is placed on the claimant of safety, which is proper.

conditions_met_evidence: Independent expert reviews converging ('Nine of the ten engineers... independently flagged the same weld joint'); conclusion is an investigation ('re-examine that joint').
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alikes apply: agreement among people who studied the question; METHOD (b) scope.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 'If you study medicine, you'll have a stable career'; C2 P denied: 'You're not studying medicine'; C3 not-Q concluded: 'so you won't have a stable career'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Speaker means 'only if': nothing suggests medicine is the only route to a stable career.

conditions_met_evidence: C2 NOT met: the restatement ('raise the minimum wage to $18 over four years, with a lower rate for businesses under 20 employees') is offered as 'As I understand your proposal' and is specific; the objection targets an actual feature (the carve-out incentive).
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: restating a view in words its holder would accept.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 linked to a disliked figure: 'praised by a dictator'; C2 offered as reason to condemn: 'anyone who supports it is basically siding with tyranny'; C3 no evidence the dictator's praise bears on the proposal's merits.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Association as real evidence about the claim: none shown. Supporters sharing the specific criticised commitment: no, supporting an economic proposal is not supporting tyranny.
notes: Ad hominem family: guilt-by-association over reductio-ad-hitlerum (no Hitler/Nazi link).

conditions_met_evidence: C1 decision about what to do next: 'we can't stop now'; C2 past unrecoverable costs cited: 'We've already spent $3 million'; C3 treated as a reason to continue regardless of future prospects: 'or all that money will be wasted', despite 'The consultants say it will never work'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Past investment as evidence the project is nearly done: no, the evidence is that it will never work. Commitment/reputation, or real remaining benefit/switching cost: none stated.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 speaker cannot imagine: 'I just can't see how something as complex as the eye could have come about through gradual steps'; C2 concluded false: 'so it can't have evolved'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Disbelief backed by a specific reason: 'complex' is given, but no reason why gradual steps cannot produce complexity.

conditions_met_evidence: C2 NOT met: popularity not treated as decisive (hedged 'probably'); C3 arguably NOT met: restaurant quality is largely a matter of diners' experience, and 3,000 reviews is a large aggregate of experience.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alikes apply: question about tastes; popular belief as some evidence.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 categorical syllogism with middle term 'had a key card': 'Everyone who took part in the burglary had a key card... Mark had a key card'; C2 middle term undistributed in both premises (predicate of an A-proposition, and of a singular affirmative); C3 conclusion links the other terms: 'So Mark was one of the burglars'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Probabilistic argument offered as mere evidence: no, stated as a conclusion ('So Mark was one of the burglars').
notes: Mark having a key card is evidence that narrows suspects; the error is treating it as proof.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 two positions: 'The union wants a 6% raise and management is offering 2%'; C2 compromise concluded: 'a 4% raise is the fair outcome'; C3 reason is only that it is between ('so').
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike may apply: 'Compromise as a practical way to reach agreement, not as a claim about truth' - in wage bargaining, splitting the difference is a common fairness convention; but 'the fair outcome' reads as a claim about what the correct wage is.
notes: Settled by: whether 'fair' means 'an acceptable bargaining compromise' (no issue) or 'the correct raise on the merits' (flag). Catalog unclear on normative 'fair' claims.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 standard stated: 'Show me one peer-reviewed study'; C2 met: 'Here are three' (and later 'Here's one' meta-analysis); C3 stricter standards demanded ('show me a meta-analysis', then 'a decade of real-world results') with reasons ('Three studies isn't enough', 'Meta-analyses can be biased') that are general and would already have applied when the standard was set.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Raising the standard for something learned after it was set (a flaw in how it was met): no specific flaw in the studies or meta-analysis is identified.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 random independent process: 'The roulette wheel'; C2 run cited: 'landed on red eight times in a row'; C3 opposite concluded due: 'so black is due'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Dependent outcomes: no. Run treated as evidence of bias: no, the bettor bets against the streak.

conditions_met_evidence: C2/C3 NOT met: the critics are not accused of acting against their own claim, and their criticism is not declared false; the speaker asks for a consistent test ('If cost per daily user is the test, they should apply it... too').
lookalikes_ruled_out: Red-herring considered: C3 NOT met - whether the critics' test is applied consistently bears on the issue. double-standard considered as the speaker's legitimate charge, not an error by the speaker.
notes: Possible issue only if read as an attempt to deflect from the stadium's cost (whataboutism); the text does not conclude the subsidy is fine.

conditions_met_evidence: C3 NOT met: each step is supported ('since payments are calculated directly from the rate'); conclusion hedged ('will likely cool demand').
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: well-supported chain.

conditions_met_evidence: C3 NOT met: the link is stated and institutional ('our bylaws say past decisions bind future ones'); conclusion is a procedural safeguard ('write down the specific circumstances').
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: well-supported chain.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 two things presented as equivalent: 'Jaywalking and armed robbery are both crimes'; C2 shared feature (being crimes) but they differ greatly in seriousness and in what they show about honesty; C3 conclusion relies on treating them as equal: 'no more trustworthy than one convicted of robbery'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Compared in the respect they really are alike: the conclusion is about trustworthiness, where they differ greatly.
notes: detect=partly: the seriousness difference is common knowledge.

conditions_met_evidence: Valid modus tollens: 'If the backup had run... there would be a file timestamped after midnight... There isn't one. So the backup did not run.'
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike: valid contrapositive form; not denying the antecedent.

lookalikes_ruled_out: N/A

conditions_met_evidence: C3 NOT met in the fallacious sense: weight carries over from parts to whole; 500 x 2 kg = 1,000 kg, stated as 'roughly'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: properties such as weight that do carry over.

conditions_met_evidence: C1 claim/advice: 'My doctor told me to quit smoking'; C2 not living up to health advice herself: 'she's overweight herself'; C3 offered as reason to dismiss: 'so I don't see why I should listen to her'.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Hypocrisy as reason for suspicion only: no, it is a reason not to listen. Question about her credibility: the advice rests on medical evidence, not on her conduct. Third-party whataboutism: no.
notes: C2 is strained: being overweight is not strictly inconsistent with 'quit smoking' (it is inconsistent only with a broader 'look after your health' message). If tu quoque is read narrowly, ad-hominem (abusive) is the label; either way the verdict is flag.

conditions_met_evidence: Randomized, placebo-controlled trial of 12,000, replicated twice; conclusion 'good evidence'. No candidate entry's conditions met.
lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alike applies: controlled comparison.

lookalikes_ruled_out: Look-alikes apply: relevant character when the question is about the person (fitness for a role); appeal-to-spite look-alike: record of fraud when deciding whether to hire.
